narrator.name: Mark Jeffrey
narrator.role: Host of the Hash Rate podcast; Partner, Stillcore Capital (a Bittensor fund); author of Bitcoin Explained Simply and The Case for Bitcoin; advisor to TAO Synergies
narrator.one_line: Serial entrepreneur and early Bitcoin author who turned his Hash Rate podcast into the most followed weekly show on Bittensor subnets, then co-founded Stillcore Capital to invest in TAO and subnet tokens, explaining the network to newcomers through Bitcoin analogies and a contest-capitalism frame.

statements.quote: Like early Bitcoin, Bittensor is hard to explain to newcomers. But the explanations and metaphors have improved over time. So it's perhaps best to take it from the top
statements.context: Opening of the State of TAO report, written for Stillcore Capital in January 2026 and posted by him as an X Article on 19 February 2026.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: Instead of forming a 'company', imagine you make a list of 'tasks'. Freelancers -- some with PhD's -- from all over the world compete to finish each task for you THE BEST. It's a contest. And only the best freelancers get paid ... But not by you. A Bitcoin-like blockchain pays them. That's Bittensor.
statements.context: His plain-language definition of Bittensor in the State of TAO report, aimed at readers who do not know the network.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: The result: Bitcoin created $2.5 trillion in value and Earth's largest supercomputer in aggregate, 500x larger than the nearest competitor. Bittensor says, Hmm. This 'task contest' mining idea worked exceedingly well once. Maybe it can be replicated across multiple AI (and other) domains. So Bittensor takes Bitcoin's mining idea and expands it. Bittensor makes mining programmable.
statements.context: State of TAO report, explaining the network as a generalisation of Bitcoin mining.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: In Bitcoin, the contest to 'find the hash of the previous block first' basically boils down to guessing the number of gumballs in a jar. ... the actual work of 'guessing gumballs' is itself very wasteful. By contrast ... the 'work' done in Bittensor mining contests is actually very useful. Bittensor calls this Proof of Useful Work.
statements.context: State of TAO report, contrasting Bitcoin hashing with subnet tasks.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: You can think of Subnets as 128 AI startups. ... To get a Subnet token, you must stake $TAO. This means that subnet tokens ARE rehypothecated $TAO under the hood. ... Subnet tokens and $TAO are simply two versions of the same thing.
statements.context: State of TAO report, explaining subnet tokens to investors and contrasting them with ERC20 tokens on Ethereum.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: Thus $TAO tracks the combined value of all the Subnets akin to how an S&P 500 ETF tracks the combined value of the world's top 500 companies. In a certain sense, all Subnets are part of a 'TAO keiretsu'. They are at once separate and distinct, but united by a super-entity, a base token, that aligns them all.
statements.context: State of TAO report, on why subnet growth accrues to TAO.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: Everything in Bittensor is contests within contests to win new $TAO. ... It's contests within contests. It's very Darwinian. It's very 'Hunger Games'. And it's merciless: the weakest subnets and the weakest miners are regularly culled by the chain. ... Every day is a new gladiatorial round.
statements.context: State of TAO report, describing daily emission competition between subnets and between miners.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: Like Bitcoin, miners can join or leave anytime. It's open to anyone, anywhere on earth. For this reason, some call Bittensor an 'Open Economy'. Others call it 'Incentivism'. We call it the most ferocious form of capitalism yet invented. Everyone competes, always. Only the most excellent get anything. And everyone is re-evaluated continuously: you cannot rest.
statements.context: State of TAO report, naming the category and setting his own label against the community's terms.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: We've seen the same fractal repeat many times in compu-history: open (aka 'The Bazaar') wins over closed, large and centralized ('the Cathedral') almost every time. ... The lesson is clear: You can't fight the whole world. Open-source movements typically attract the best minds from all over the world to contribute.
statements.context: State of TAO report, arguing why a subnet could reach a $1B market cap, with TCP/IP, Linux, Android and Bitcoin as precedents.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: Bittensor Subnets are 'open source startups'. Anyone can join one of these startups by becoming a Miner. And anyone can invest in them by buying Subnet tokens. Because the whole world competes, you get this insanely efficient product creation engine.
statements.context: State of TAO report, on why subnet products ship faster and cheaper than company products.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: Over the last four years, Bittensor wallets have been like early Bitcoin or Ethereum wallets: ganky, not consumer-ready, and difficult for consumers (even crypto-savvy consumers) to use or understand. ... It's been the same ~20,000 participants trading against each other for the last year. ... No new money was entering. That just changed.
statements.context: State of TAO report, criticising the network's tooling before praising the December 2025 Crucible and Tao.com wallets.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: At Stillcore, we suspect we will see one or more breakout subnets in 2026. We think at least one Subnet token will reach a market cap of $1B. ... If this occurs, the demand for $TAO will spike rapidly. Why? Because you need $TAO to get Subnet tokens. $TAO is the coin of the realm.
statements.context: State of TAO report section titled Subnets In 2026: The 'ICO Phase'?, comparing subnets to the 2016 to 2017 Ethereum ICO wave.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: Bittensor has the exact same economics as Bitcoin, by design. This includes a halving at roughly 4-year intervals. ... Nobody knows exactly what the halving will do to Bittensor's price. But if Bitcoin is comparable, that suggests a 10x or a 20x over 2026 is possible (that would put $TAO price at $3000 - $6000).
statements.context: State of TAO report, on the 15 December 2025 halving, with Bitcoin's 2012 to 2013 run as the comparison.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: Previously, the mechanism was based on Subnet token price: whoever had the highest price won the most new $TAO. But this allowed early winners that had already achieved high market caps to rest. A 'liquidity aristocracy' arose. Inertia supplied them with a moat. ... The chain is generous – and it is savage and merciless.
statements.context: State of TAO report, explaining the TAO Flow emission change of early 2026 and why he approves of it.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: At this time, Bittensor does not have a true competitor. Bittensor was fair-launched, just like Bitcoin. This is extremely hard to pull off, and now serves as a significant moat – one that could probably not be replicated today.
statements.context: State of TAO report, on competition; he adds that no entity owns more than 1% of TAO, which he calls fairer than Bitcoin.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: At this time, no Subnet has truly crossed the chasm. True, there is a lot of early success and 'signal'. But no Subnet has yet achieved true breakaway success. ... But we don't know yet if Subnet teams can productize and market products. We don't know whether they can generate breakout revenue.
statements.context: State of TAO report, stating the risks of the Stillcore thesis.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: When you abstract everything away, Bittensor is all about adding an ownership layer and aligning incentives in a decentralized environment. This effectively creates a new form of capitalism. And we think it's the most ferocious form of capitalism. Whole companies and whole departments can be atomized, broken down into their component pieces, and reassembled in the image of Bitcoin's Incentivism.
statements.context: Conclusion of the State of TAO report.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: Once the subnet cap is lifted and we can have more than 128 Subnets, we'll likely see an explosion of new ideas and Subnets. 'Bittensor is a Y-Combinator that anyone can join,' as our friends at Unsupervised Capital recently put it in their 'The Investment Case For Bittensor' report. We agree. And we're betting on it.
statements.context: Final lines of the State of TAO report, adopting another fund's frame and stating his own position.

source.title: State of TAO - A Bittensor Report (Excerpt)
source.outlet: Mark Jeffrey on X (Stillcore Capital report)

statements.quote: My $TAO vibe-miner is an attempt to create the Bittensor version of this. ... A Claw, on Bittensor hosting ... with its own TAO wallet ... It pays for its own life. ... many (most?) subnets require 'human alpha' to win: no Claw or Claude can yet match that.

It's the most efficient form of capitalism ever invented

statements.quote: But Sam is not a key man for this ecosystem. The researchers who did the technical work, the miners who contributed compute, the validators who evaluated quality, they all remain, and Bittensor is 128 subnets, 482,000+ wallets, and an ecosystem of builders who are not going anywhere. One actor left the stage. The production continues.
statements.context: From The Show Goes On (TAO), a Stillcore Capital X Article published the day after Covenant AI founder Sam Dare exited Bittensor; signed by the fund he co-runs, not by him alone.

statements.quote: Does TAO have governance defects? Yes. Does it need to become more decentralized? Yes, and Const has acknowledged this openly, with reforms underway for months. But the way to address those concerns is to build, not to rug your own investors and wrap a cash grab in the language of principle.
statements.context: Same Stillcore Capital article, conceding the governance critique while rejecting Sam Dare's exit; signed by the fund, not by him alone.

foundation.mission.summary: Bittensor takes Bitcoin's mining contest and makes it programmable: a chain pays the best freelancers in the world to complete useful tasks, adding an ownership layer and aligned incentives to open work.

foundation.vision.summary: Companies and departments get atomised and reassembled as open source startups anyone can join or invest in, with an explosion of subnets once the cap lifts.

foundation.values.summary: Merciless, continuous competition: no dead weight, no resting on past wins, the weakest culled daily by a chain that is generous and savage at once; governance defects are to be fixed by building, not by walking away.

problem.cultural.summary: Closed, large, centralised systems lose to open ones throughout computing history; you cannot fight the whole world.

problem.market.summary: AI commodities are hard to monetise, Bittensor's wallets were unusable for years so no new money entered, and no subnet has yet crossed the chasm into breakout revenue.

problem.institutional.summary: The 2024 wallet hack, a liquidity aristocracy under early dTAO, and the Covenant founder's exit are the institutional stresses he names, each answered by the network's response rather than by doubt in the design.

opportunity.summary: The first halving, consumer wallets arriving in December 2025, an expected $1B subnet that would pull attention and TAO demand the way ICOs pulled ETH, and public-market vehicles now offering exposure.

audience.summary: Newcomers who find the network hard to grasp, and investors and holders told to keep score in TAO and accumulate it as if it were 2013 Bitcoin; subnet builders are addressed through weekly Hash Rate interviews.

positioning.category.summary: A Bitcoin-like asset and the possible third great coin; the Linux and the actual OpenAI of AI; an S&P 500 ETF of AI startups; above all the most ferocious form of capitalism yet invented.

positioning.differentiator.summary: Proof of useful work instead of gumball guessing, subnet tokens that are rehypothecated TAO so value flows back to the base asset, and a fair launch that cannot be repeated.

positioning.reason.summary: Bitcoin already proved the contest model at $2.5 trillion scale; open beats closed in every prior era; the halving and the subnet ICO phase give a reason to expect repricing.

positioning.against.summary: OpenAI and centralised AI giants, Scale AI, VC-funded startups, and the Covenant founder whose exit he treats as a cash grab rather than a principled critique.

value.functional.summary: Cheaper AI products built faster by self-recruiting global miners, subnet tokens backed by staked TAO, and a first $100M subnet nine weeks after dTAO.

value.emotional.summary: He points to the unique community and heart of the network as its felt appeal.

value.self_expressive.summary: Joining means competing rather than taking a job, and he models it by running his own autonomous vibe-miner and reporting its failures.

messaging.h1.summary: Bittensor makes mining programmable and is the most ferocious form of capitalism yet invented; TAO today is where Bitcoin was in 2013, so accumulate it.

messaging.proof.summary: Price moves (up 130% in a month), the first $100M subnet, subnets beating incumbents on cost, and Bitcoin's own halving history.

voice.summary: Enthusiast's capitals and exclamation marks in show notes, vivid violent metaphors in long form, and candid admissions of what does not yet work.

relationship.summary: Podcast host turned fund partner and public-company advisor who says he is betting on the network, and who also mines it with his own agent.

language.term.summary: He adopts Dynamic Tao and dTAO early as a marketplace for subnet rewards, coins TAO keiretsu and liquidity aristocracy, relays Proof of Useful Work, and rejects Open Economy and Incentivism in favour of ferocious capitalism.

coinages.meaning: Subnets as separate firms united and aligned by the base token
Early high-market-cap subnets that could rest on inertia before TAO Flow

coinages.term: the most ferocious form of capitalism
coinages.meaning: His preferred label for Bittensor's continuous contest economy, offered instead of Open Economy or Incentivism
Economics of paying only the winners of open contests
Subnets using other subnets for inference or storage so cost savings compound (in the State of TAO report)
An autonomous agent that mines subnets and pays for its own hosting in TAO

genealogy.summary: He arrives as a podcaster and evangelist, framing TAO as a Bitcoin-like asset that could reach a trillion and as the Linux or actual OpenAI of the space [mark-jeffrey-001] [mark-jeffrey-004], relaying the third great coin idea from a guest [mark-jeffrey-006] and previewing Dynamic Tao as a marketplace for subnet rewards before it shipped [mark-jeffrey-008]. The register is show notes and headlines rather than argument.

As a Stillcore partner he writes the long-form State of TAO, replacing headline analogies with a worked model: freelancer contests, programmable mining, subnets as AI startups tracked by TAO like an S&P ETF, and the most ferocious form of capitalism [mark-jeffrey-012] [mark-jeffrey-016] [mark-jeffrey-018]. He criticises the wallets and the lack of a breakout subnet [mark-jeffrey-021] [mark-jeffrey-026], and during the Covenant exit concedes governance defects while defending the network and Const [mark-jeffrey-032]. Accumulate TAO like 2013 Bitcoin becomes the investor line [mark-jeffrey-033].
genealogy.shift: From evangelist headlines to an investor's model with named risks; the Bitcoin comparison moves from price analogy to mechanism analogy.

genealogy.summary: Now an advisor to a public TAO holding company, he compresses the thesis to Bittensor is where Bitcoin was in 2013, early, misunderstood, and inevitable [mark-jeffrey-034], while Hash Rate turns to bridges, TAO as a reserve currency, and subnet tokens reaching other chains [mark-jeffrey-035].
genealogy.shift: The audience widens to public-market investors; the 2013 Bitcoin frame becomes the single repeated sentence.
